title: Virtual Clinical / Imaging Trials: Concept and Components
source: Abadi et al., J Med Imaging 7(4):042805, 2020
content: A virtual clinical trial (VCT), also called a virtual imaging trial (VIT) or in silico imaging trial, replaces some or all of the physical elements of an imaging study with computational models. The review by Abadi, Segars, Tsui, Kinahan, Bottenus, Frangi, Maidment, Lo and Samei (Journal of Medical Imaging, 2020) argues that conventional clinical imaging trials are often impractical because of ethical limits (for example extra radiation dose), cost, duration, and the lack of ground truth: in a real patient the exact size, location and composition of a lesion are rarely known with certainty. A VCT has three core components. (1) Computational phantoms, the virtual patients, which model anatomy and optionally physiology and pathology such as inserted lesions. (2) Imaging simulators, which model the physics of the acquisition device (for CT: x-ray source spectrum, bowtie filter, detector response, scatter, noise, and reconstruction). (3) Interpretation models or virtual readers, which may be mathematical model observers, CAD/AI algorithms, or human readers reading simulated images. Because every element is controlled, a VCT has perfect ground truth and can be repeated systematically across scanner settings, dose levels and patient populations. This lets researchers isolate the effect of one factor, such as lesion diameter or reconstruction kernel, while holding everything else constant. The review covers applications across several modalities. A companion editorial in the same issue, 'Virtual clinical trials: why and what' (Samei, Kinahan, Nishikawa, Maidment), gives the motivation. For an AI stress-testing framework, the VCT structure maps directly onto three parts: generating virtual patients with designed lesions, simulating or synthesizing scanner-specific images, and treating the AI model under test as the 'reader'.

title: Toward Widespread Use of Virtual Trials (AAPM TG387 Perspective)
source: Abadi et al., Med Phys 51(12):9394-9404, 2024
content: 'Toward widespread use of virtual trials in medical imaging innovation and regulatory science' was published in Medical Physics (vol. 51, issue 12, December 2024, pp. 9394-9404; online October 2024). It has 15 authors, including Ehsan Abadi, Bruno Barufaldi and Ehsan Samei. The paper is a consensus-style overview based on the ongoing work of an American Association of Physicists in Medicine task group, TG387. It names three core requirements a virtual imaging trial framework must meet before it can be broadly trusted. Credibility: the models of patients, scanners and readers must be validated well enough for the question being asked, which links to regulatory credibility frameworks such as ASME V&V 40 and the FDA guidance on computational modeling. Reproducibility: simulation configurations, random seeds, phantoms and software versions must be documented so other groups can repeat the trial. Accessibility: tools and virtual populations should be available to the community rather than locked inside single labs. These requirements apply directly to any generative-AI-based virtual trial platform. A credible implementation should log every generation parameter (lesion size, lobe, texture type, scanner profile, random seed, model version), report how realistic the synthetic images are against real data, state the context of use, and keep the generated cohorts and evaluation code reproducible. The paper treats VITs as a complement to clinical evidence in imaging innovation and regulatory science, not as a wholesale replacement.

title: FDA VICTRE: First All-in-Silico Imaging Trial (Breast DBT vs DM)
source: Badano et al., JAMA Netw Open 2018
content: VICTRE (Virtual Imaging Clinical Trial for Regulatory Evaluation) was published by Badano and colleagues at the US FDA in JAMA Network Open in 2018 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.5474). It is the best-known demonstration that a regulatory-style imaging comparison can be run entirely in silico. The trial asked whether digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) outperforms digital mammography (DM) for lesion detection, a question previously studied in a human comparative trial submitted to FDA. VICTRE simulated 2,986 virtual patients using computational breast phantoms with inserted lesions. In silico versions of both imaging systems produced the images using GPU-accelerated Monte Carlo x-ray transport (MC-GPU), and a computational reader (a model observer) interpreted them. The endpoint was the difference in area under the ROC curve (delta-AUC) between modalities. Using a fully-crossed design, the trial was sized for a standard error of 0.01 in delta-AUC, half the uncertainty of the human comparative trial. The in silico result agreed in direction with the human trial, favoring DBT. The authors present in silico trials as a way to complement or reduce traditional clinical trials, not to replace them outright. All in silico components (phantom generation, lesion models, MC-GPU, reconstruction, reader) were released openly. For iTRIALSPACE, VICTRE is the canonical precedent: it shows that sizing, endpoints, and pre-specified statistical analysis can be carried out with virtual patients. Its pipeline is physics-based rather than generative-AI-based.

title: VICTRE Pipeline and MC-GPU Monte Carlo X-ray Simulator
source: DIDSR VICTRE pipeline docs; Badal & Badano, Med Phys 36:4878-4880, 2009
content: The FDA Division of Imaging, Diagnostics and Software Reliability (DIDSR) packages the VICTRE tools as a Python 'Pipeline' class. The documented steps are breast phantom generation, compression, cropping, mass (lesion) generation, lesion insertion, MC-GPU projection, DBT reconstruction, and extraction of lesion-present and lesion-absent regions of interest. Each step is configured through argument dictionaries (for example arguments_generation, arguments_mcgpu, arguments_recon). A random seed and results folder support reproducibility, and projection can be sent to a GPU host while reconstruction runs on a CPU host. The code is released under CC0, except the filtered back-projection code, which derives from GPL3 code and stays GPL3. The FDA Catalog of Regulatory Science Tools lists the pipeline as a tool for generating in silico breast images to evaluate DM and DBT devices. MC-GPU, the x-ray transport engine, was described by Badal and Badano in Medical Physics (2009, vol. 36, pp. 4878-4880). It adapts the PENELOPE 2006 photon interaction physics and material data to CUDA GPUs, models photon transport in voxelized geometries (electron transport is not simulated), and is reported to run about 15-40 times faster than a single CPU core, depending on the source. Code is at github.com/DIDSR/MCGPU and DIDSR/VICTRE_MCGPU. The pipeline pattern is directly relevant to a CT virtual trial tool: phantom, lesion model, insertion, physics projection, reconstruction, and ROI/reader analysis are separable, seeded, configurable stages. An agentic orchestrator (for example LangGraph) can mirror these stages as graph nodes.

title: XCAT Computational Phantoms (4D Extended Cardiac-Torso)
source: Segars et al., Med Phys 37(9):4902-4915, 2010; Segars et al., Med Phys 2013
content: The 4D extended cardiac-torso (XCAT) phantom, described by Segars et al. in '4D XCAT phantom for multimodality imaging research' (Medical Physics 2010; 37(9):4902-4915), is a whole-body computational model of human anatomy and physiology widely used as the virtual patient in imaging simulation. Its organ surfaces are defined with non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS) and subdivision surfaces built from segmentations of the National Library of Medicine Visible Male and Female datasets and patient data. These were transformed to match 50th-percentile male and female body measurements and organ volumes. Parameterized cardiac and respiratory motion models, derived from gated multislice CT, make the phantom 4D, so it can simulate breathing and heartbeat. Because the surfaces are mathematical, the phantom can be voxelized at any resolution and deformed to represent different body sizes. The original paper demonstrated simulations in PET, SPECT and CT. A 2013 Medical Physics paper by Segars et al. introduced a library of anatomically variable 4D XCAT adult phantoms based on chest-abdomen-pelvis CT of normal patients from the Duke database, giving a population of virtual patients rather than a single reference anatomy. XCAT phantoms are developed at Duke University and are commonly combined with CT simulators such as DukeSim. In a VIT, lesions such as lung nodules can be inserted into the phantom's lung parenchyma with known size, shape and composition, which gives exact ground truth. Compared with generative-AI synthesis, phantom-based approaches give strong physical control and interpretability, but can look less like real clinical images in fine texture.

title: DukeSim: Scanner-Specific CT Simulation Platform
source: Abadi et al., IEEE Trans Med Imaging 38(6):1457-1465, 2019; Shankar et al., Med Phys 2022
content: DukeSim is a CT simulation framework from Duke University, described by Abadi et al. in 'DukeSim: a realistic, rapid, and scanner-specific simulation framework in computed tomography' (IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging, vol. 38, no. 6, 2019, pp. 1457-1465). It projects voxelized computational phantoms such as XCAT by combining ray-tracing for primary signal with Monte Carlo simulation for scatter, which lets it model specific commercial scanner geometries and components rapidly. In the original validation with the Mercury phantom on a Siemens Somatom Definition Flash, relative errors between real and simulated images were under about 3% for contrast, noise magnitude, noise texture and spatial resolution. Later work extended and further validated the platform. A 2019 paper extended it to photon-counting CT. Jadick et al. (Physics in Medicine and Biology, 2021) added tube current modulation, with validation on a SOMATOM Force. Shankar et al. (Medical Physics, 2022) validated it with an anthropomorphic chest phantom on two Siemens scanners (Force and Flash) across 28 dose and reconstruction conditions. DukeSim illustrates the physics-based route to scanner variation: rather than learning vendor 'style' from data, it models the acquisition chain explicitly, so changes in dose, kernel or geometry follow physical laws. For an AI stress-testing platform, this is the gold-standard way to vary the scanner protocol. A generative pipeline that claims to emulate vendors or protocols should ideally be checked against physics-based simulation or phantom measurements of noise (NPS) and resolution (MTF/TTF).

title: M-SYNTH: FDA Knowledge-Based In Silico Dataset for Evaluating Mammography AI
source: Sizikova et al., NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks
content: M-SYNTH, from Sizikova and colleagues at FDA's Center for Devices and Radiological Health, appeared in the NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks track ('Knowledge-based in silico models and dataset for the comparative evaluation of mammography AI'). It is a close precedent for using in silico data to stress-test AI rather than to train it. Stochastic digital breast models, with and without lesions, were imaged by a digital replica of an acquisition system using Monte Carlo x-ray simulation in the public VICTRE toolkit. The dataset systematically varies four breast fibroglandular density categories, lesion (mass) properties, and exposure levels from 20% to 100% of the clinically recommended dose. The FDA catalog describes it as about 45,000 synthetic digital mammography examples. Using M-SYNTH, the authors showed controlled performance trends for a detection AI: performance decreased as breast density increased, increased as mass density increased, and fell as exposure dropped, with the best results at exposures somewhat below the nominal recommended dose for each breast type. Realism was checked by comparing pixel-intensity statistics against the real INbreast dataset. The FDA catalog states explicitly that M-SYNTH cannot fully replace real patient data for evaluating mammography AI. The data are on Hugging Face (didsr/msynth). For iTRIALSPACE the M-SYNTH design is the template to follow: factorial variation of patient, lesion and acquisition factors, then per-factor performance curves for the model under test. The key difference is that iTRIALSPACE substitutes generative synthesis of chest CT for physics simulation of mammography.

title: Projection-Domain Lesion Insertion into Patient CT Data
source: Chen, Yu, Leng, Yu, McCollough, Proc SPIE 9412:94121R, 2015
content: Lesion insertion creates hybrid images: real patient scans with digitally added lesions of known size and location. Mayo Clinic researchers (Chen, Yu, Leng, Yu, McCollough; Proc SPIE 2015) developed projection-domain insertion. Lesion models segmented from patient images are forward-projected (Siddon ray tracing, using a Siemens Definition Flash geometry), converted from HU to linear attenuation, added to the patient's raw projection data, and reconstructed. Because the lesion passes through the same reconstruction as the patient data, its appearance correctly reflects scan and reconstruction parameters. The authors showed that inserted lesions changed appearance between FBP (B40f) and iterative (SAFIRE I40f) reconstructions, which image-domain insertion cannot easily reproduce. In phantom tests CT numbers matched within 1 HU, and in a small reader check radiologists could not tell inserted from real lesions. The main limitation is that the method needs vendor raw data, which few researchers have. Mayo later extended the approach to lung nodules (32 nodules from 21 patients), liver lesions validated by radiologists, dual-source dual-energy CT (Ferrero et al., Med Phys 2018), and photon-counting CT. Lesion insertion is a third route alongside phantom simulation and pure generative synthesis. Image-domain insertion (pasting or blending a lesion into reconstructed slices) is easy but ignores noise and resolution consistency. Projection-domain insertion is physically faithful but needs raw data. Generative inpainting (for example ControlNet- or diffusion-based) learns realistic texture and blending but has weaker physical guarantees. An iTRIALSPACE implementation should state which route it uses and check consistency of noise and sharpness between lesion and background.

title: ControlNet: Adding Spatial Conditional Control to Diffusion Models
source: Zhang, Rao, Agrawala, ICCV 2023 (arXiv 2302.05543)
content: ControlNet (Lvmin Zhang, Anyi Rao, Maneesh Agrawala; 'Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models', ICCV 2023, pp. 3836-3847; arXiv February 2023) is a neural architecture for adding spatial conditioning to a large pretrained diffusion model without degrading it. Example conditions include edge maps, depth maps, segmentation masks and human pose. The method locks (freezes) the parameters of the pretrained diffusion model and creates a trainable copy of its encoding layers. The copy receives the conditioning image, and its outputs are added back into the frozen network through 'zero convolutions': 1x1 convolutions whose weights and biases start at zero. Because they start at zero, the ControlNet branch adds nothing at initialization, so fine-tuning starts from the exact behavior of the pretrained model and harmful noise gradients are avoided early in training. The connections grow from zero as training proceeds. The authors demonstrated ControlNet with Stable Diffusion using single or multiple conditions, with or without text prompts, and reported robust training on both small (under 50k images) and large (over 1M images) datasets. In medical imaging, ControlNet is the standard way to make a generative model obey a segmentation mask. For example, NVIDIA's MAISI uses a 3D ControlNet so that a CT volume is generated to match a given multi-organ mask, which can include a tumor label. For iTRIALSPACE, the 'programmable' part of the virtual patient is the conditioning mask: drawing a sphere or lobulated shape of a given diameter in a chosen lung lobe, then letting a mask-conditioned generator render realistic CT around it.

title: Latent Diffusion Models (Stable Diffusion Foundation)
source: Rombach et al., CVPR 2022 (arXiv 2112.10752)
content: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) were introduced by Rombach, Blattmann, Lorenz, Esser and Ommer in 'High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models' (CVPR 2022). They are the basis of Stable Diffusion. Pixel-space diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising random noise, but training them can take hundreds of GPU-days and inference is expensive because it needs many sequential network evaluations. LDMs first train an autoencoder that compresses images into a lower-dimensional latent space that keeps perceptually important content, then train the diffusion model in that latent space. This sharply reduces compute while keeping quality. Conditioning on text, bounding boxes, class labels or other inputs is added through cross-attention layers in the denoising U-Net. The paper reported state-of-the-art results for inpainting and class-conditional synthesis and competitive results on unconditional generation, text-to-image and super-resolution. Code is at github.com/CompVis/latent-diffusion. Latent diffusion is the dominant design for 3D medical image synthesis, because a full chest CT volume (for example 512 x 512 x 300 voxels) is too large for direct pixel-space diffusion on typical GPUs. NVIDIA MAISI follows this pattern: a 3D volume compression network (VAE) maps CT to a latent, a 3D latent diffusion model generates latents conditioned on attributes such as voxel spacing and body region, and a ControlNet adds mask conditioning. Key failure modes relevant to virtual trials are hallucinated anatomy, loss of fine texture or small structures in the compressed latent, and memorization of training data. Each should be assessed before synthetic cases are used as test sets.

title: NVIDIA MAISI: Medical AI for Synthetic Imaging (3D CT Generation)
source: Guo et al., WACV 2025 (arXiv 2409.11169)
content: MAISI (Medical AI for Synthetic Imaging), by Pengfei Guo and colleagues at NVIDIA (arXiv 2409.11169; WACV 2025, pp. 4430-4441), is a diffusion-based framework for generating high-resolution synthetic 3D CT volumes with paired segmentation masks. It addresses data scarcity, annotation cost and privacy. MAISI has three 3D networks. (1) A volume compression network (VAE), trained on 39,206 CT volumes, encodes CT into a latent space and decodes it back. (2) A latent diffusion model, trained on 10,277 CT volumes, generates latents conditioned on body region and voxel spacing. (3) A ControlNet adds conditional control, for example generation from a segmentation mask or inpainting. Conditioning masks cover up to 127 anatomical structures, so outputs come with annotations. Outputs reach up to 512 x 512 x 768 voxels with flexible dimensions and spacing. A tensor-splitting parallelism scheme reduces memory for large 3D convolutions. The released MAISI label dictionary (132 labels) includes 'lung tumor' (label 23), the five lung lobes (left upper 28, left lower 29, right upper 30, right middle 31, right lower 32) and airway (132). This makes it possible in principle to place a tumor mask inside a chosen lobe and generate matching CT through the ControlNet. The tutorials document a 'controllable_anatomy_size' option and recommend output dimensions divisible by 16. MAISI is the most directly relevant open component for iTRIALSPACE. Note that MAISI conditions on anatomy and geometry, not on scanner vendor or reconstruction kernel, so protocol variation needs a separate mechanism (physics-based noise or kernel simulation, or a fine-tuned conditional model).

title: MAISI Releases, Licenses and Hardware Requirements (MONAI / NV-Generate-CTMR)
source: Project-MONAI tutorials (generation/maisi); NVIDIA-Medtech NV-Generate-CTMR repository
content: MAISI was first released through MONAI tutorials (generation/maisi). That folder is now marked deprecated (October 2025) in favor of the NVIDIA-Medtech NV-Generate-CTMR repository. Versions: MAISI v1 'maisi3d-ddpm' (August 2024) uses a DDPM noise scheduler with about 1000 inference steps and requires body-region conditioning. MAISI v2 'maisi3d-rflow' (March 2025) uses a rectified-flow scheduler, which the documentation says speeds up latent diffusion inference by about 33x (around 30 steps). It drops the body-region requirement and adds a modality input. The VAE is shared between versions. NV-Generate-CTMR also lists MRI models (rflow-mr, rflow-mr-brain) and a body-mask generator. Inference configuration includes voxel spacing, output size (each dimension divisible by 16, e.g. 512x512x256), an anatomy_list of labels to generate, and controllable_anatomy_size pairs (structure name plus a 0-1 size scale; the documented example is a small hepatic tumor). The tutorial documents ControlNet fine-tuning with a kidney tumor example, and lung tumor is a label in the shared label dictionary. Documented GPU memory: at least 16 GB for 512x512x128 inference and training; 24 GB inference and 40 GB training at 512x512x512. Peak inference memory on A100-80GB ranges from about 15 GB (256x256x128) to about 50 GB (512x512x768). Licensing: source code is Apache-2.0. Weight licenses differ by model (the MONAI tutorial lists NSCLv1; NV-Generate-CTMR lists NVIDIA Open Model or Non-Commercial licenses), so check them before commercial use. A browser-based MVP cannot run MAISI client-side. A realistic architecture calls a GPU inference service or uses precomputed cohorts.

title: MONAI Generative Models Extension
source: Pinaya et al., arXiv 2307.15208, 2023
content: 'Generative AI for Medical Imaging: extending the MONAI Framework' by Walter H. L. Pinaya and colleagues (arXiv 2307.15208, July 2023) introduced MONAI Generative Models, an open-source extension of the MONAI framework (official implementation originally at github.com/Warvito/generative_monai, with components later integrated into MONAI core). Its motivation is that diffusion models, autoregressive transformers and GANs are complex to implement, which has slowed adoption and made fair comparison hard. The package provides standardized, modular implementations of these model families, including diffusion model U-Nets, noise schedulers and inferers, latent diffusion with autoencoders (VQ-VAE and KL autoencoders), ControlNet, and perceptual and adversarial losses. It works in 2D and 3D and was demonstrated on CT, MRI and X-ray data across several anatomical regions. The paper reproduces published studies in a standardized way, ships pre-trained models, and describes five experiments covering out-of-distribution detection, image-to-image translation and super-resolution. Design goals were modularity and extensibility for long-term maintenance. MONAI Generative is the toolkit layer beneath NVIDIA MAISI, which is built on the same MONAI generative components. For a team building a real iTRIALSPACE system, these building blocks allow (a) fine-tuning a mask-conditioned ControlNet specifically for lung nodules on LIDC-IDRI-derived masks, (b) training lesion-focused inpainting models, and (c) using generative models as out-of-distribution detectors to flag synthetic cases that are implausible.

title: MedSyn: Text-Guided Anatomy-Aware 3D Lung CT Synthesis
source: Xu et al., IEEE Trans Med Imaging 2024 (arXiv 2310.03559)
content: MedSyn ('MedSyn: Text-guided Anatomy-aware Synthesis of High-Fidelity 3D CT Images', Yanwu Xu, Li Sun, Wei Peng and coauthors; IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging 2024, doi:10.1109/TMI.2024.3415032) generates full 3D lung CT volumes conditioned on free-text radiology report content. The authors note that earlier diffusion models were limited to low-resolution outputs. MedSyn uses a hierarchical scheme built on a modified U-Net: it first generates a low-resolution volume from text, then uses later generators to produce the full-resolution volume. To keep anatomy plausible, it generates vascular, airway and lobular segmentation masks together with the CT image, so the output is anatomy-aware rather than texture-only. The authors report better performance than GAN and diffusion baselines, especially on fissure lines, airways and vascular structures, supported by blind evaluation by 10 board-certified radiologists (per the arXiv version). Code is at github.com/batmanlab/MedSyn under a CC-BY-NC (non-commercial) license. Relative to MAISI, MedSyn represents a text-conditioned approach (for example describing findings in report language) rather than explicit mask-conditioned placement. For a programmable virtual trial, text conditioning is convenient but imprecise: a prompt such as '8 mm nodule in right upper lobe' does not guarantee the exact diameter or position. Mask conditioning gives verifiable ground truth. A practical design uses an LLM to parse a natural-language trial specification into structured parameters (diameter_mm, lobe, nodule type, scanner profile), then converts these into masks and conditioning for a mask-conditioned generator.

title: Label-Free Liver Tumor Segmentation via Synthetic Tumors
source: Hu et al., CVPR 2023 (arXiv 2303.14869)
content: 'Label-Free Liver Tumor Segmentation' by Qixin Hu, Yixiong Chen, Junfei Xiao, Shuwen Sun, Jieneng Chen, Alan L. Yuille and Zongwei Zhou (CVPR 2023, pp. 7422-7432) showed that a segmentation model can learn to segment liver tumors without any manual tumor annotations, by training only on synthetic tumors inserted into healthy CT scans. The synthesis is model-free and rule-based rather than a deep generative network. It selects a location inside the liver while avoiding vessels, generates a tumor shape (ellipsoid-based with elastic deformation), creates texture from processed noise matched to tumor intensity, and post-processes to mimic effects such as mass effect and a capsule-like boundary. The authors reported that models trained on these synthetic tumors reached performance similar to models trained on real annotated tumors. They also emphasized that synthesis can produce many small or tiny tumors, which are rare in real datasets but clinically important for early detection. Code is at github.com/MrGiovanni/SyntheticTumors. Lessons for iTRIALSPACE: (1) Controllable synthesis of lesion size is valuable precisely because small lesions are under-represented in real data, and evaluating detection sensitivity as a function of diameter is a core stress test. (2) Realism must be validated, for example with reader studies or Visual Turing Tests, because unrealistic synthetic lesions give misleading performance estimates. (3) Inserting lesions into real healthy CT keeps realistic background anatomy and noise. Lung nodule analogues would insert solid, part-solid or ground-glass nodules into lung parenchyma, avoiding vessels and fissures.

title: DiffTumor: Towards Generalizable Tumor Synthesis
source: Chen et al., CVPR 2024 (arXiv 2402.19470)
content: 'Towards Generalizable Tumor Synthesis' by Qi Chen, Xiaoxi Chen, Haorui Song, Zhiwei Xiong, Alan Yuille, Chen Wei and Zongwei Zhou (CVPR 2024, pp. 11147-11158), known as DiffTumor, uses diffusion models to synthesize tumors in abdominal CT. The paper builds on the observation that early-stage tumors (under 2 cm) look similar on CT whether they arise in the liver, pancreas or kidney. A diffusion model trained on a limited number of tumor examples from a single organ can therefore generate realistic tumors in other organs. In DiffTumor, a diffusion model, operating in a learned latent space and conditioned on a tumor mask and surrounding context, inpaints tumor texture into healthy organ regions. Segmentation and detection models (for example nnU-Net and Swin UNETR) trained with these synthetic tumors generalized to real tumors across varied patient demographics, imaging protocols and institutions. The supplementary material includes a reader study, a Visual Turing Test, and comparisons with the earlier rule-based synthesis of Hu et al. 2023 using tumor-wise sensitivity. Code is at github.com/MrGiovanni/DiffTumor. For lung nodule virtual trials, DiffTumor shows that (a) mask-conditioned diffusion inpainting is a practical way to place lesions of controlled size into real scans, (b) small lesions are where synthetic data adds most value, and (c) cross-institution and cross-protocol evaluation should be part of the validation. The same mask-plus-context inpainting approach could be applied to lung parenchyma, with the conditioning mask defining nodule diameter and lobe.

title: LeFusion: Lesion-Focused Diffusion for Controllable Lung Nodule Synthesis
source: LeFusion, ICLR 2025 (arXiv 2403.14066)
content: LeFusion ('LeFusion: Controllable Pathology Synthesis via Lesion-Focused Diffusion Models', ICLR 2025; arXiv 2403.14066) generates lesion-containing image-mask pairs from lesion-free images, and was validated on lung nodule CT from LIDC-IDRI and on cardiac MRI. Its main design choice is a lesion-focused training objective: the diffusion loss is computed only inside the lesion region. During sampling, background context comes from the forward-diffused original image, so the anatomy outside the lesion is preserved rather than re-generated. A companion lesion-mask diffusion component generates diverse masks, which gives control over nodule size, location and boundary shape. The LIDC portion used 1,010 chest CT scans with 2,624 nodule regions of interest, plus 3,076 normal ROIs from healthy regions for augmentation. Adding LeFusion-generated data improved downstream segmentation with nnU-Net and SwinUNETR. Related later work (2025-2026 preprints) reports that diffusion models still struggle with small (under 10 mm), low-contrast, subsolid or juxtapleural nodules. These are exactly the hard cases that Lung-RADS and Fleischner thresholds focus on (6 mm, 8 mm, 15 mm). For iTRIALSPACE, lesion-focused inpainting is arguably the best-matched generative design: background anatomy and scanner noise come from a real clinical scan (preserving a realistic vendor and kernel texture), while the nodule is synthesized inside a mask whose diameter and lobe location are set by the trial specification. The realism of small and subsolid synthetic nodules should be validated separately before drawing conclusions about AI sensitivity at those sizes.

title: GAN-Based CT Lung Nodule Synthesis (3D Conditional GAN)
source: Jin et al., MICCAI 2018 (arXiv 1806.04051)
content: Before diffusion models, generative adversarial networks (GANs) were the main approach for synthesizing lung nodules. Dakai Jin, Ziyue Xu and colleagues at NIH, in 'CT-Realistic Lung Nodule Simulation from 3D Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks for Robust Lung Segmentation' (MICCAI 2018; arXiv 1806.04051), trained a 3D conditional GAN on over 1,000 nodules from LIDC. The generator takes a volume of interest whose central region has been erased and fills it with a nodule that blends into the surrounding lung tissue, which is effectively 3D inpainting. A multi-mask reconstruction loss improves realism and blending at the boundary. The authors used the synthetic nodules to create hard training cases, nodules touching the lung border, where the progressive holistically-nested network (P-HNN) lung segmentation model failed. Training with these cases improved segmentation in those situations. Other GAN-based work has generated ground-glass nodules and diverse nodule appearances for detector augmentation. Compared with diffusion models, GANs sample faster (a single forward pass) but are prone to mode collapse (low diversity) and training instability. They also offer less fine control over attributes unless explicitly conditioned. Diffusion and latent diffusion models now dominate because of better sample quality and diversity, and because they integrate easily with mask conditioning (ControlNet) and inpainting. For a stress-testing platform, the key point from the GAN literature is the use case: synthesized hard cases (juxtapleural, juxtavascular, small, subsolid) reveal systematic failure modes of segmentation and detection models that random test sets under-sample.

title: LIDC-IDRI: Lung Image Database Consortium Thoracic CT Collection
source: Armato et al., Med Phys 38(2):915-931, 2011; TCIA
content: The Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI), described by Armato et al. in Medical Physics (2011; 38(2):915-931, doi:10.1118/1.3528204), is the most widely used public chest CT dataset for lung nodule research. The paper describes 1,018 cases, each with a clinical thoracic CT scan and an XML file of annotations from four experienced thoracic radiologists. The TCIA collection page lists 1,010 subjects, 244,527 images and about 133 GB, including some DX/CR radiographs, under a CC BY 3.0 license (DOI 10.7937/K9/TCIA.2015.LO9QL9SX). Annotation used a two-phase process. In the blinded phase, each radiologist independently marked lesions as 'nodule >= 3 mm', 'nodule < 3 mm', or 'non-nodule >= 3 mm'. In the unblinded phase, each radiologist reviewed their own marks alongside the anonymized marks of the other three and gave a final opinion; consensus was not forced. 7,371 lesions were marked as nodules by at least one radiologist. Of these, 2,669 were marked 'nodule >= 3 mm' by at least one radiologist, and 928 (34.7%) of those received that mark from all four. For nodules >= 3 mm, readers provided outlines (contours) and subjective ratings of characteristics such as subtlety, calcification, sphericity, margin, lobulation, spiculation, texture and malignancy likelihood. LIDC-IDRI is the parent of LUNA16, the training source for many nodule synthesis models (for example LeFusion, GAN-based nodule simulation), and partly underlies TotalSegmentator's lung_nodules task. Its scanners and protocols are heterogeneous, which makes it useful for kernel and slice-thickness stratification.

title: LUNA16 Nodule Detection Challenge and Dataset
source: Setio et al., Med Image Anal 42, 2017 (arXiv 1612.08012)
content: LUNA16 (LUng Nodule Analysis 2016), described by Setio et al. in 'Validation, comparison, and combination of algorithms for automatic detection of pulmonary nodules in computed tomography images: the LUNA16 challenge' (Medical Image Analysis, 2017), is the standard benchmark for pulmonary nodule detection. It uses 888 CT scans from LIDC-IDRI, chosen by excluding scans with slice thickness greater than 2.5 mm and scans with inconsistent slice spacing or missing slices. The reference standard is the 1,186 nodules >= 3 mm accepted by at least 3 of the 4 LIDC radiologists. Nodules marked by fewer readers, nodules < 3 mm, and non-nodules are 'irrelevant findings': detections on them count as neither true nor false positives. The data are distributed in ten subsets for 10-fold cross-validation. There were two tracks: complete nodule detection, and false-positive reduction on a provided candidate set. The primary metric is the Competition Performance Metric (CPM): the average sensitivity at seven predefined false-positive rates per scan (1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4 and 8), read from the FROC curve. Top systems used convolutional neural networks, and combining systems achieved sensitivity above 95% at fewer than 1.0 false positives per scan. An observer study found that the best systems detected nodules missed by the original expert annotators. For iTRIALSPACE, LUNA16's protocol is a natural evaluation template: report the FROC curve and CPM on synthetic cohorts, then stratify sensitivity by designed nodule diameter, lobe, type and scanner profile.

title: National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) and Its CT Collection
source: NLST Research Team, N Engl J Med 365:395-409, 2011; TCIA NLST collection
content: The National Lung Screening Trial (NLST) randomized 53,454 high-risk current or former heavy smokers at 33 US centers to three annual screens with low-dose CT (26,722) or single-view chest radiography (26,732). Enrollment ran from August 2002 to April 2004. Results (N Engl J Med 2011;365:395-409) showed lung cancer mortality of 247 vs 309 deaths per 100,000 person-years, a 20% relative reduction with low-dose CT (95% CI 6.8-26.7%), and a 6.7% reduction in all-cause mortality. Both arms had high false-positive rates. NLST is the evidence base behind US lung cancer screening and the Lung-RADS reporting system. The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA) hosts the NLST imaging (version 3, September 2021): low-dose chest CT for 26,254 subjects (73,116 studies, over 21 million images, about 11 TB), digitized histopathology for 451 subjects, and a publicly distributable subset of clinical data, under CC BY 4.0 (DOI 10.7937/TCIA.HMQ8-J677). The full clinical dataset is available through NCI's Cancer Data Access System (CDAS). NLST scans came from multiple vendors and reconstruction kernels at screening dose. This makes the collection valuable as real background anatomy for lesion insertion or generation in low-dose settings, for studying domain shift across vendors and kernels, and as a large real-world reference distribution for checking that synthetic screening CTs are realistic. The scale and download size mean an MVP should use a small curated subset or metadata only.

title: DeepLesion: Large-Scale Multi-Lesion CT Dataset (NIH Clinical Center)
source: Yan, Wang, Lu, Summers, J Med Imaging 5(3):036501, 2018
content: DeepLesion, described by Ke Yan, Xiaosong Wang, Le Lu and Ronald Summers in the Journal of Medical Imaging (2018, vol. 5, no. 3, 036501), is a large public dataset of lesions in CT. The NIH Clinical Center built it by mining 'bookmarks' that radiologists made in its PACS during routine reporting. These bookmarks include RECIST-style long- and short-axis diameter measurements and bounding boxes. The dataset contains 32,735 lesions on 32,120 axial CT slices from 10,594 studies of 4,427 unique patients, with 1-3 lesions per annotated slice. It is a 'universal' lesion dataset: lesions include lung nodules, liver tumors, enlarged lymph nodes, kidney, bone and soft-tissue lesions. Annotations are sparse (only the bookmarked slice is labeled; other lesions in the volume may be unannotated). The original paper reported a universal lesion detector reaching 81.1% sensitivity at five false positives per image. Relevance to iTRIALSPACE: DeepLesion offers real-world, clinically measured lesion size distributions, useful as a prior when sampling the diameters of synthetic lesions so designed cohorts can match or deliberately depart from clinical distributions. It also provides lung lesions in diagnostic (often contrast-enhanced) rather than screening CT, which is a different domain from LIDC-IDRI and NLST. It is a good resource for domain-shift testing, though incomplete labeling means false-positive counts against DeepLesion are biased upward.

title: Medical Segmentation Decathlon - Lung Tumour Task (Task06)
source: Antonelli et al., Nat Commun 13:4128, 2022 (arXiv 2106.05735)
content: The Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD), reported by Antonelli et al. in Nature Communications (2022, 13:4128) and first described as arXiv 1902.09063, was a challenge held at MICCAI 2018 that tested whether a single algorithm could generalize across ten different segmentation tasks without human tuning. One of the ten is Task06_Lung: segmentation of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) tumors on thoracic CT, with images sourced from The Cancer Imaging Archive. It is a single-label task (tumor vs background). It is known for small, low-contrast targets and few labeled cases (the publicly labeled training set is commonly reported as 63 volumes, with additional unlabeled test scans held out for the challenge), which makes it hard. The MSD tasks are distributed openly (including via the AWS Open Data registry). The decathlon helped popularize self-configuring methods: nnU-Net was a leading entry and later formed the basis of many public tools. Relevance to iTRIALSPACE: unlike LIDC-IDRI (mostly small screening-type nodules with multi-reader marks), MSD Lung contains larger, clinically confirmed primary tumors with voxel-level segmentation masks. This makes it useful for (a) training or validating mask-conditioned generators on the appearance of malignant lesions, (b) evaluating segmentation (Dice, surface distance) as well as detection, and (c) a 'real-tumor' reference set for checking that synthetic tumors share appearance statistics with real NSCLC.

title: TotalSegmentator: Whole-Body CT Anatomy Segmentation Tool and Dataset
source: Wasserthal et al., Radiol Artif Intell 5(5):e230024, 2023; GitHub wasserth/TotalSegmentator
content: TotalSegmentator (Wasserthal et al., 'TotalSegmentator: Robust Segmentation of 104 Anatomic Structures in CT Images', Radiology: Artificial Intelligence 2023; 5(5):e230024) is an open nnU-Net-based tool that segments major anatomical structures in CT. The original paper trained on 1,204 CT examinations from 2012, 2016 and 2020 at University Hospital Basel, covering 104 structures (27 organs, 59 bones, 10 muscles, 8 vessels). It reported a test Dice of 0.943 and outperformed another public model on an external dataset (Dice 0.932 vs 0.871). The annotated dataset is public on Zenodo (doi 10.5281/zenodo.6802613). Version 2 expanded the default 'total' task to 117 classes. Lung-relevant classes include lung_upper_lobe_left, lung_lower_lobe_left, lung_upper_lobe_right, lung_middle_lobe_right and lung_lower_lobe_right, plus trachea and other thoracic structures. A separate 'lung_nodules' task segments lung and lung nodules and was trained on 1,353 subjects, partly from LIDC-IDRI. Install with 'pip install TotalSegmentator' (Python >= 3.10, PyTorch >= 2.0). Open tasks are Apache-2.0. Some additional tasks need a license that is free for non-commercial use. For iTRIALSPACE, TotalSegmentator is a key enabler. Lobe masks let the system place a synthetic nodule mask inside a requested lobe (sampling a center point within the lobe mask, eroded so the nodule does not cross the pleura or fissure unless juxtapleural placement is intended). It can also check generated volumes for anatomical plausibility (for example, lobe volumes within normal ranges) and assign a lobe to each detection when computing per-lobe sensitivity of the AI under test.

title: LNDb: Lung Nodule Database with Fleischner Follow-Up Labels
source: Pedrosa et al., arXiv 1911.08434, 2019; LNDb challenge
content: LNDb ('LNDb: A Lung Nodule Database on Computed Tomography', Pedrosa et al., arXiv 1911.08434) contains 294 chest CT scans collected retrospectively at Centro Hospitalar e Universitario de Sao Joao (CHUSJ) in Porto, Portugal, between 2016 and 2018. Inclusion criteria were based on LIDC-IDRI. Scans with intravenous contrast or slice thickness greater than 1 mm were excluded. Five radiologists, each with at least 4 years of experience, annotated the scans in a single-blinded way with no consensus or review step. Annotations include nodule centroids, segmentations and subjective characterization following LIDC-style ratings. The associated LNDb Challenge covered nodule detection, segmentation, texture characterization (solid, part-solid, ground-glass), and prediction of patient follow-up according to the 2017 Fleischner Society guidelines, with 58 CTs held out as a test set. A 2024 Scientific Data paper released additional nodule characteristics (calcification, lobulation, malignancy, spiculation, subtlety). Data are hosted on Zenodo and the LNDb grand-challenge site. Relevance to iTRIALSPACE: LNDb is a European single-center dataset, which makes it a useful external domain relative to US-centric LIDC-IDRI and NLST. Its nodule texture labels support evaluation stratified by nodule type. Its Fleischner follow-up labels connect detection and measurement to clinical management. This is the right framing for a virtual trial: a 1-2 mm measurement error near a 6 mm or 8 mm threshold changes the recommended management.

title: Supporting Datasets: AbdomenAtlas-8K and the Mayo/AAPM Low-Dose CT Data
source: Qu et al., NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv 2305.09666); McCollough et al., Med Phys 44(10), 2017
content: Two further datasets are useful around a chest-CT virtual trial. AbdomenAtlas-8K (Chongyu Qu, Zongwei Zhou and colleagues; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks) annotated spleen, liver, kidneys, stomach, gallbladder, pancreas, aorta and IVC in 8,448 CT volumes (about 3.2 million slices) from at least 26 hospitals. It used an active-learning procedure combining multiple pretrained segmentation models, automatic error detection, and attention guidance for annotators. The authors estimated that conventional manual annotation would take an experienced annotator about 1,600 weeks, versus three weeks with their procedure. The same group produced the synthetic-tumor work (SyntheticTumors, DiffTumor), and AbdomenAtlas demonstrates large-scale, multi-institutional CT curation. Data and code are at github.com/MrGiovanni/AbdomenAtlas. It is abdominal, so mainly relevant as a curation model and for multi-organ generation. The 2016 NIH-AAPM-Mayo Clinic Low Dose CT Grand Challenge provided routine-dose and simulated quarter-dose data from contrast-enhanced abdominal CT (30 patients: 10 training, 20 test), with liver lesion detection as the task (McCollough et al., Medical Physics 2017, vol. 44, issue 10). The cases were later released in a common projection data format, and Moen et al. (Medical Physics 2021) published a broader 'Low-dose CT image and projection dataset' on TCIA. Paired full- and reduced-dose data are the standard resource for validating dose-reduction simulation and denoising. For iTRIALSPACE, they are a reference for checking that a 'low-dose protocol' variation produces realistic noise magnitude and texture.

title: MONAI: Open-Source Framework for Medical Imaging Deep Learning
source: Cardoso et al., arXiv 2211.02701, 2022
content: MONAI (Medical Open Network for AI), described in 'MONAI: An open-source framework for deep learning in healthcare' (M. Jorge Cardoso and 56 coauthors, arXiv 2211.02701, November 2022), is a PyTorch-based, community-supported, consortium-led framework for medical imaging AI (pip install monai). It extends PyTorch with medical-specific data handling: loading DICOM and NIfTI through readers such as ITK and pydicom-based loaders, dictionary-based transforms that keep images and labels spatially aligned, orientation and spacing normalization, intensity windowing for CT Hounsfield units, and patch-based sampling. It also provides sliding-window inference for large 3D volumes, network architectures (U-Net, SegResNet, UNETR, Swin UNETR, RetinaNet-style 3D detectors), losses, metrics (Dice, Hausdorff, surface distance, FROC-related utilities), and workflow engines. The ecosystem includes MONAI Label (interactive annotation), MONAI Deploy (clinical deployment packaging), a Model Zoo of 'bundles' (pretrained models with configs, including a lung nodule CT detection bundle trained on LUNA16-style data), and generative components on which NVIDIA MAISI is built. For iTRIALSPACE, MONAI is the natural backbone of a real implementation. It loads and resamples CT consistently, runs MAISI generation, hosts the 'AI under test' (for example a MONAI Model Zoo lung nodule detector) behind a uniform inference interface, and computes evaluation metrics. A Next.js/LangGraph.js front end would call a Python service built on MONAI rather than running these models in Node.js.

title: nnU-Net: Self-Configuring Segmentation Framework
source: Isensee et al., Nat Methods 18:203-211, 2021
content: nnU-Net, by Isensee, Jaeger, Kohl, Petersen and Maier-Hein ('nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation', Nature Methods 2021; 18(2):203-211; online December 2020), is a segmentation framework that configures itself for a new dataset without manual intervention. From a 'dataset fingerprint' (image sizes, voxel spacings, intensity distributions, modality), it uses fixed parameters, interdependent heuristic rules and empirical decisions to set preprocessing (resampling, CT intensity clipping and normalization), network topology (2D, 3D full-resolution, and 3D cascade U-Nets), patch and batch size, training schedule, data augmentation, and post-processing. It can ensemble configurations via cross-validation. Without manual tuning, nnU-Net surpassed most existing approaches, including highly specialized solutions, on 23 public datasets from international segmentation competitions, including Medical Segmentation Decathlon tasks. It is now the default strong baseline in medical segmentation, and many public tools are built on it, including TotalSegmentator. Relevance to iTRIALSPACE: (1) nnU-Net is a realistic 'AI under test' for lung tumor or nodule segmentation (for example trained on MSD Task06 Lung or LIDC-IDRI masks), whose Dice and detection sensitivity can be measured as a function of designed nodule diameter, texture and scanner profile. (2) Synthetic-tumor papers such as Hu et al. 2023 and DiffTumor used nnU-Net backbones to measure the downstream value of synthetic data. (3) Its sensitivity to voxel spacing and intensity normalization makes it a good probe for protocol-related domain shift.

title: TorchIO: Medical Image Preprocessing and Augmentation (Artifact Simulation)
source: Perez-Garcia, Sparks, Ourselin, Comput Methods Programs Biomed 208:106236, 2021
content: TorchIO (Fernando Perez-Garcia, Rachel Sparks, Sebastien Ourselin; Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine 2021, 208:106236; arXiv 2003.04696) is an open-source Python library for efficient loading, preprocessing, augmentation and patch-based sampling of 3D medical images in PyTorch. It represents images as 'Subject' objects that keep image volumes, label maps and metadata (spacing, orientation, affine) together, so spatial transforms are applied consistently. Transforms include spatial operations (resampling, cropping or padding, random affine and elastic deformation, flips) and intensity operations (rescaling, Z-normalization, random noise, blur, gamma). It also includes artifact simulations that originated in MRI: motion (k-space), ghosting, spikes and bias field. The library supports patch-based training and inference with queues and aggregators for volumes too large for GPU memory. For iTRIALSPACE, TorchIO is a lightweight way to implement acquisition-style perturbations in the image domain, for example adding Gaussian noise to approximate reduced dose, Gaussian blur to approximate a smoother kernel, or resampling to emulate thicker slices. It is also used for consistent resampling of generated volumes and masks. These image-domain perturbations are approximations, however. Real CT noise is spatially correlated with a kernel-dependent noise power spectrum, and real dose reduction changes noise in projection space. A credible scanner/protocol simulation should match noise texture (NPS) and resolution (MTF/TTF), not just add white noise. TorchIO is suitable for an MVP, while physics-based simulation is preferable for regulatory-grade claims.

title: SimpleITK and pydicom: CT I/O, Geometry and Resampling
source: Yaniv et al., J Digit Imaging 31(3):290-303, 2018; pydicom project
content: SimpleITK is a simplified, multi-language interface (Python, R, C++, others) to the Insight Toolkit (ITK) for image registration, segmentation, filtering and resampling. Yaniv, Lowekamp, Johnson and Beare described its Jupyter-notebook-based educational and reproducible-research environment in the Journal of Digital Imaging (2018; 31(3):290-303), with notebooks on GitHub (InsightSoftwareConsortium/SimpleITK-Notebooks, Apache 2.0). SimpleITK images carry physical metadata (origin, spacing, direction cosines), which is essential for CT. Nodule diameters in millimeters, lesion placement in a lobe, and comparison of detections with ground truth all depend on correct voxel-to-physical transforms. Typical operations include reading DICOM series into 3D volumes, resampling to isotropic spacing (for example 1 mm), connected-component analysis to count and size lesions, computing equivalent sphere diameter from a mask volume (d = (6V/pi)^(1/3)), and writing NIfTI or MHA files. pydicom is the standard pure-Python library for reading and writing DICOM files and their headers. It exposes tags critical for protocol stratification in a virtual trial: Manufacturer, ManufacturerModelName, ConvolutionKernel, SliceThickness, KVP, Exposure/CTDIvol, PixelSpacing, RescaleSlope and RescaleIntercept (to convert stored values to Hounsfield units). For iTRIALSPACE, these tools turn synthetic volumes into DICOM-like objects with an explicit 'scanner profile' and parse real DICOM to build stratified reference sets. Any reported measurement should be computed in physical millimeters, never in voxels.

title: Open CT Projection/Reconstruction Libraries: LEAP, ASTRA Toolbox, ODL
source: Kim & Champley, arXiv 2307.05801 (LEAP); van Aarle et al., Opt Express 24(22):25129, 2016 (ASTRA); ODL docs
content: Physics-faithful protocol variation (dose, kernel, slice thickness, geometry) needs forward projection and reconstruction, and three open libraries cover most needs. LEAP (LivermorE AI Projector for Computed Tomography), from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and introduced by Hyojin Kim and Kyle Champley ('Differentiable Forward Projector for X-ray Computed Tomography', arXiv 2307.05801), is a C++/CUDA library with a Python interface. It provides matched forward and back projector pairs that model finite voxel and detector-pixel size, flexible 3D geometries, analytic (FBP) and iterative reconstruction, multi-GPU and multi-core CPU execution, and PyTorch bindings for differentiable projection, which allows data-consistency layers in deep learning reconstruction. The ASTRA Toolbox (van Aarle et al., 'Fast and flexible X-ray tomography using the ASTRA Toolbox', Optics Express 2016) offers GPU-accelerated 2D and 3D projection primitives callable from Python and MATLAB. Its algorithms include FBP, SIRT, SART and CGLS, and it supports parallel, fan and cone-beam geometries. It is GPLv3-licensed (v2.3 released February 2025). ODL (Operator Discretization Library), developed at KTH Stockholm with CWI Amsterdam, is a Python framework for inverse problems. It wraps physical models as operators, includes optimization solvers (CGLS, BFGS, Douglas-Rachford), and binds to external projectors such as ASTRA (MPL-2.0 license). For iTRIALSPACE, a physically grounded way to emulate a low-dose protocol on a synthetic or real image is: forward-project, add Poisson noise to the transmitted intensities at a reduced photon count, then reconstruct with FBP using a chosen filter (smooth vs sharp) to emulate kernel differences. This produces correlated, kernel-dependent noise texture, unlike simple image-domain white noise.

title: LangChain.js / LangGraph.js as Orchestration for an Agentic Virtual Trial
source: LangChain LangGraph documentation (JavaScript)
content: LangGraph (with a JavaScript/TypeScript implementation, LangGraph.js) is a library from LangChain for building stateful, multi-step LLM applications as graphs. A StateGraph defines a typed shared state; nodes are functions that read the state and return updates; edges define fixed transitions, and conditional edges route to the next node based on the state. Checkpointers persist state snapshots per thread, which supports resuming runs, memory across sessions, and human-in-the-loop pauses where a user reviews or edits state before execution continues. Streaming emits intermediate state updates and tokens to a UI. LangChain.js supplies the surrounding components: chat model wrappers, prompt templates, structured output parsing (for example Zod schemas), document loaders, text splitters, embeddings, vector stores and retrievers for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). In an iTRIALSPACE demo, the graph maps onto the virtual trial workflow. (1) Parse a natural-language trial request into a structured, validated specification (lesion diameters in mm, lobes, nodule types, scanner vendors, kernels, dose levels, cohort size). (2) Retrieve guideline and methodology context (Lung-RADS thresholds, FROC/CPM definitions) via RAG to ground design choices. (3) Validate the design (for example flag diameters below 3 mm, which LIDC-style reference standards do not count as nodules). (4) Call generation and inference services. (5) Compute stratified metrics with confidence intervals. (6) Write a report with citations. The heavy imaging computation should run in Python GPU services. The LLM layer handles planning, validation and explanation, and should never fabricate numeric results.

title: Lung-RADS v2022: Categories and Size Thresholds
source: ACR Lung-RADS v2022 (summarized by Radiopaedia)
content: Lung-RADS, from the American College of Radiology, standardizes reporting and management of lung cancer screening low-dose CT (LDCT). It was updated to v2022. Categories: 0 (incomplete): prior CTs being located, lungs partially imaged, or findings suggesting an infectious or inflammatory process. 1 (negative): no nodules, or nodules with benign calcification (complete, central, popcorn, concentric rings) or fat; annual LDCT. 2 (benign appearance, <1% malignancy): solid nodule <6 mm at baseline or new <4 mm; part-solid <6 mm total diameter at baseline; ground-glass (non-solid) nodule <30 mm; juxtapleural nodule <10 mm with smooth margins and oval, lentiform or triangular shape; subsegmental airway nodule; annual LDCT. 3 (probably benign, 1-2%): solid 6 to <8 mm at baseline or new 4 to <6 mm; part-solid >=6 mm total with solid component <6 mm; ground-glass >=30 mm; 6-month LDCT. 4A (suspicious, 5-15%): solid 8 to <15 mm at baseline, growing <8 mm, or new 6 to <8 mm; part-solid with solid component 6 to <8 mm; segmental or more proximal airway nodule; 3-month LDCT, with PET/CT an option if there is a solid component >=8 mm. 4B (very suspicious, >15%): solid >=15 mm at baseline, or new or growing >=8 mm; part-solid with solid component >=8 mm; diagnostic chest CT, PET/CT and/or tissue sampling. 4X: a category 3 or 4 nodule with additional features that increase suspicion, such as spiculation, ground-glass nodule doubling in size within a year, or enlarged regional lymph nodes; managed as 4B. The 'S' modifier flags significant non-lung-cancer findings. For iTRIALSPACE, the 6, 8 and 15 mm boundaries are natural strata for designed nodule diameters.

title: Lung-RADS Measurement Rules and v1.1 / v2022 Changes
source: ACR Lung-RADS v1.1 and v2022 (summarized by Radiopaedia)
content: Lung-RADS measurement conventions matter for any system that converts a designed lesion size into a clinical category, or that scores an AI's size measurement. Nodules are measured on lung windows. The long and short axes are measured to one decimal place and the mean diameter is reported to one decimal place (v1.0 rounded to whole millimeters). A round nodule needs only one measurement. For part-solid nodules, management depends on both total diameter and the diameter of the solid component. Growth is defined as an increase in mean diameter of more than 1.5 mm, and v2022 specifies assessing growth over a 12-month interval. The most suspicious nodule determines the overall category. Version 1.1 (2019) raised the ground-glass nodule threshold from 20 mm to 30 mm, split category 4 into 4A and 4B, removed the 'C' modifier for prior lung cancer, added smooth oval, lentiform or triangular (perifissural-type) solid nodules <10 mm to category 2, and allowed a 1-month LDCT for new large nodules that may be infectious. Version 2022 added classification of atypical pulmonary cysts (category 3, 4A or 4B depending on wall thickness, multilocularity and growth), renamed 'perifissural' to 'juxtapleural' and 'endobronchial' to 'airway' nodules, made follow-up timing depend on category, kept slowly growing ground-glass nodules (<=1.5 mm growth over 12 months) in category 2, and allowed category 0 for some presumed infectious or inflammatory findings. Practical implication: an AI that measures a true 7.9 mm solid nodule as 8.1 mm moves it from category 3 to 4A, so a virtual trial should report measurement bias near thresholds, not just detection.

title: Fleischner Society 2017 Guidelines for Incidental Pulmonary Nodules
source: MacMahon et al., Radiology 284(1), 2017
content: The Fleischner Society 2017 guidelines (MacMahon et al., Radiology 2017, doi:10.1148/radiol.2017161659) cover incidentally detected pulmonary nodules in adults. They replaced the 2005 solid-nodule and 2013 subsolid-nodule guidelines, raised the minimum size threshold for routine follow-up, and merged both into one table. They do not apply to patients 35 years or younger, patients with known cancer, immunocompromised patients, or lung cancer screening (which uses Lung-RADS). Single solid nodule: <6 mm, no routine follow-up for low-risk patients, with optional CT at 12 months for high-risk patients; 6-8 mm, CT at 6-12 months, then consider (low risk) or perform (high risk) CT at 18-24 months; >8 mm, consider CT at 3 months, PET/CT or tissue sampling. Multiple solid nodules 6-8 mm: CT at 3-6 months for all patients, with management then guided by the most suspicious nodule. Single ground-glass nodule: <6 mm, no routine follow-up; >=6 mm, CT at 6-12 months, then if persistent every 2 years until 5 years. Single part-solid nodule >=6 mm: CT at 3-6 months, then if persistent with solid component <6 mm, annual CT for 5 years (a persistent solid component >=6 mm is highly suspicious). Multiple subsolid nodules: <6 mm, CT at 3-6 months; >=6 mm, CT at 3-6 months, then management by the most suspicious nodule. Measurement: nodules 3-10 mm are recorded as the average of long and short axes on the same slice, rounded to the nearest millimeter. Nodules <3 mm are called micronodules and are not measured. Thin sections (<=1.5 mm, ideally 1 mm) are recommended, and significant growth is >=2 mm.

title: Lung Lobe Anatomy for Nodule Location
source: Radiopaedia 'Lungs'; TotalSegmentator lobe classes
content: The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, lower) and the left lung has two (upper and lower). Each lung has an oblique (major) fissure. The right lung also has a horizontal (minor) fissure separating the upper and middle lobes, which the left lung lacks. The lingula is part of the left upper lobe (with superior and inferior lingular segments) and is the left-sided counterpart of the right middle lobe. There are 10 bronchopulmonary segments on the right and 8 on the left in common descriptions. Fissures may be incomplete, which matters for lobe segmentation algorithms. Location matters clinically and for AI evaluation. Upper-lobe location is a recognized malignancy risk factor: it is a predictor in the Brock (PanCan) nodule malignancy model, and Fleischner allows follow-up of small solid nodules in high-risk patients partly on the basis of suspicious morphology or upper-lobe location. Detection difficulty also varies by location: juxtapleural nodules (touching the pleura), perifissural nodules, juxtavascular nodules, and nodules near the diaphragm or hilum are common sources of false negatives and segmentation errors. Automated lobe masks are available in TotalSegmentator (lung_upper_lobe_left, lung_lower_lobe_left, lung_upper_lobe_right, lung_middle_lobe_right, lung_lower_lobe_right) and in the MAISI label dictionary (labels 28-32). For iTRIALSPACE, lobe should be a first-class trial parameter. Designed nodules are placed inside a chosen lobe mask, AI detections are mapped back to lobes, and per-lobe sensitivity is reported to expose location-dependent failure modes.

title: Nodule Types (Solid, Part-Solid, Ground-Glass) and Malignancy Risk Factors
source: McWilliams et al., N Engl J Med 369:910-919, 2013; Fleischner 2017; Lung-RADS v2022
content: Pulmonary nodules are classified by attenuation. Solid nodules completely obscure the underlying lung structures (vessels and bronchial walls). Ground-glass (non-solid, pure ground-glass) nodules increase attenuation but leave vessels and bronchial walls visible. Part-solid nodules contain both ground-glass and solid components. Part-solid and ground-glass nodules together are called subsolid. Persistent subsolid nodules are associated with the adenocarcinoma spectrum and are often slow-growing, which is why Fleischner and Lung-RADS give them longer follow-up and separate size thresholds. Lung-RADS puts ground-glass nodules <30 mm in category 2, while for part-solid nodules the solid-component size drives escalation (6 to <8 mm: 4A; >=8 mm: 4B). Fleischner notes that part-solid nodules cannot reliably be distinguished as such below 6 mm. Morphology also matters: spiculation is a strong suspicious feature (Lung-RADS 4X), while benign calcification patterns and fat suggest benignity. The Brock (PanCan) model (McWilliams et al., NEJM 2013; 12,029 nodules in 2,961 participants, 144 malignant) identified older age, female sex, family history of lung cancer, emphysema, larger nodule size, upper-lobe location, part-solid type, lower nodule count and spiculation as predictors of malignancy. For iTRIALSPACE, nodule type is a key stress axis. Ground-glass and part-solid nodules have low contrast against lung parenchyma, and detection and segmentation AIs, as well as generative models, often struggle with them. Synthetic cohorts should vary type independently of size, and report results separately for solid, part-solid and ground-glass nodules.

title: FROC Analysis, Sensitivity at FPs/Scan, and the LUNA16 CPM
source: Setio et al., Med Image Anal 2017; Chakraborty, FROC methodology (RJafroc)
content: Lesion detection tasks, where a scan can contain zero or several lesions and the system must localize them, are evaluated with free-response ROC (FROC) analysis rather than standard ROC. Each detection (mark) is scored as a lesion localization (true positive) if it falls within an acceptance criterion of a true lesion, or a non-lesion localization (false positive) otherwise. In LUNA16, a candidate counts as a hit if it lies within the radius of a reference nodule. Multiple hits on one nodule count once, and hits on 'irrelevant findings' are ignored. Sweeping the detection confidence threshold traces the FROC curve: lesion-level sensitivity on the y-axis against mean false positives per scan on the x-axis. The LUNA16 Competition Performance Metric (CPM) summarizes the curve as the mean sensitivity at 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 4 and 8 false positives per scan. Clinically, operating points around 1-4 FPs/scan are often discussed. The choice of acceptance radius is somewhat arbitrary and affects results, so it must be pre-specified and reported. Chakraborty and colleagues developed the AFROC and JAFROC figures of merit and jackknife methods for statistical comparison of FROC data, implemented in the R package RJafroc, which also supports comparisons of AI systems with readers. For a virtual trial with known ground truth, FROC/CPM should be computed overall and per stratum (diameter bin, lobe, nodule type, scanner/kernel/dose). Lesion-level sensitivity per stratum is the most interpretable stress-test output, for example: 'sensitivity at 1 FP/scan falls from X for 8-15 mm solid nodules to Y for 4-6 mm ground-glass nodules'.

title: Confidence Intervals for Sensitivity: Wilson Score and Bootstrap
source: Brown, Cai, DasGupta, Statistical Science 16(2):101-133, 2001
content: Virtual trials often produce many small strata (for example 4-6 mm ground-glass nodules in the right middle lobe on a sharp kernel), so uncertainty must be reported for every metric. For a binomial proportion such as sensitivity (detected lesions / total lesions), Brown, Cai and DasGupta ('Interval Estimation for a Binomial Proportion', Statistical Science 2001) showed that the textbook Wald interval (p +/- z*sqrt(p(1-p)/n)) has erratic and often poor coverage, even for fairly large n, and fails badly near 0 or 1. They recommend the Wilson score interval (introduced by Wilson in 1927) or the equal-tailed Jeffreys interval for small n, and the Agresti-Coull interval for larger n. The Wilson interval is centered at (p + z^2/2n)/(1 + z^2/n), with half-width z*sqrt(p(1-p)/n + z^2/4n^2)/(1 + z^2/n), and stays inside [0,1]. For metrics without simple closed-form variance, such as CPM, FROC-derived sensitivity at a fixed FP rate, AUC, or the Dice distribution, the nonparametric bootstrap is standard: resample at the correct unit (usually patients or scans, not individual lesions, because lesions within a scan are correlated), recompute the metric, and take percentile or BCa intervals from 1,000-10,000 replicates. Differences between conditions (for example vendor A vs vendor B) should use paired bootstrap when the same virtual patients are imaged under both conditions. This pairing is a major statistical advantage of virtual trials, because it removes patient-to-patient variability from the comparison. Report the n per stratum alongside every interval.

title: Subgroup and Stratified Analysis; Hidden Stratification
source: Oakden-Rayner, Dunnmon, Carneiro, Re, ACM CHIL 2020 (arXiv 1909.12475)
content: Aggregate performance can hide clinically important failures. Oakden-Rayner, Dunnmon, Carneiro and Re ('Hidden Stratification Causes Clinically Meaningful Failures in Machine Learning for Medical Imaging', ACM CHIL 2020) defined hidden stratification as poor performance on an unlabeled subset of cases. It arises when the meaningful variation in a dataset is incompletely described, for example a cancer detector with high overall accuracy that misses a rare aggressive subtype. They showed that such subsets can have low prevalence, low label quality, subtle features or spurious correlates, and that relative performance differences can exceed 20% on clinically important subsets. They concluded that evaluating hidden stratification should be a critical part of any ML deployment in medical imaging. Virtual imaging trials address this directly: the strata are designed rather than discovered, so every subgroup (nodule diameter bin, lobe, nodule type, juxtapleural or juxtavascular location, vendor, kernel, slice thickness, dose level, patient size) can be populated with enough cases. Good practice is to pre-specify the strata and primary endpoint before running, use balanced factorial or Latin-hypercube designs to separate effects, report per-stratum metrics with confidence intervals and n, and correct for multiple comparisons or treat subgroup findings as hypothesis-generating. Interaction effects matter too: a model may handle small nodules on smooth kernels but fail on small nodules with sharp kernels at low dose. Regression models of detection probability (for example logistic regression on diameter, type, kernel and dose) summarize these effects compactly.

title: Multi-Reader Multi-Case (MRMC) Studies and the FDA iMRMC Tool
source: FDA iMRMC software (Gallas); CRAN iMRMC package
content: Multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) studies are the standard design for evaluating imaging devices and AI-assisted reading. Several readers (for example radiologists) each interpret the same set of cases under two or more conditions, such as unaided vs AI-aided or modality A vs modality B. In a fully crossed design every reader reads every case in every condition. Both readers and cases are random effects, so variance estimates must account for reader variability, case variability and their correlations. Ignoring this underestimates uncertainty, so conclusions would not generalize to new readers and new patients. Established analysis methods include Dorfman-Berbaum-Metz (DBM) and Obuchowski-Rockette (OR) ANOVA-based methods, and U-statistic variance estimators developed at FDA by Gallas and colleagues. The FDA's iMRMC software (R package iMRMC, version 2.1.0 on CRAN in 2024, maintained by Brandon Gallas) performs MRMC analyses of AUC and other metrics. It handles fully crossed and arbitrary (split-plot, missing-data) designs, returns variance estimates, confidence intervals and p-values, and also supports sizing new studies. The VICTRE trial used a fully crossed design with computational readers, sized for a standard error of 0.01 in delta-AUC. For iTRIALSPACE, MRMC thinking applies even when the 'reader' is an AI model. Multiple AI models (or random seeds or versions) can play the role of readers, synthetic patients are the cases, and imaging conditions are the modalities. A future human-reader extension (radiologists reading synthetic cases with and without AI) would need formal MRMC analysis.

title: Domain Shift Across Scanners, Kernels and Dose; CT Harmonization
source: Mali et al., J Pers Med 11(9):842, 2021
content: Medical AI models often lose performance when the acquisition domain changes: a different scanner vendor or model, reconstruction kernel (smooth vs sharp), reconstruction algorithm (FBP vs iterative vs deep-learning reconstruction), slice thickness, dose level, contrast phase, or patient population. CT texture and noise depend strongly on these factors, so learned features can shift even when anatomy is identical. In radiomics the problem is well documented. Mali et al. ('Making Radiomics More Reproducible across Scanner and Imaging Protocol Variations: A Review of Harmonization Methods', Journal of Personalized Medicine 2021) group harmonization approaches into image-domain methods (standardized acquisition protocols, post-processing of raw data, data augmentation, and image-to-image translation or style transfer such as GAN-based kernel conversion) and feature-domain methods (feature selection for robustness, normalization, and statistical batch-effect correction such as ComBat, originally from genomics). Harmonization can reduce shift but can also remove signal or introduce artifacts, so it must itself be validated. For AI stress testing, the key point is that real-world test sets rarely contain enough controlled variation to estimate how much each factor contributes. A virtual imaging trial can hold patients and lesions fixed while varying one acquisition factor at a time, producing a 'robustness profile' (for example sensitivity vs kernel, vs dose, vs vendor). This is the core value proposition of iTRIALSPACE. The credibility of these profiles depends on how faithfully the synthetic pipeline reproduces real vendor and kernel characteristics, which should be checked against real multi-vendor data or physical phantom measurements.

title: Reconstruction Kernel Effects and Kernel Conversion
source: Choe et al., Radiology 292:365-373, 2019
content: The reconstruction kernel (convolution filter in filtered back-projection, or the equivalent setting in iterative reconstruction) trades spatial resolution against noise. Smooth (soft-tissue) kernels suppress high-frequency noise and blur edges, while sharp (lung or bone) kernels preserve fine detail such as small nodule margins and airway walls but greatly amplify noise and shift the noise power spectrum toward higher frequencies. Vendors use different naming schemes (for example Siemens B30f/B50f/B70f, GE STANDARD/LUNG/BONE, Philips B/C/L/YA, Canon FC-series), so kernel names are not comparable across vendors. Lung screening protocols often reconstruct both a soft and a sharp series. Kernel choice measurably changes quantitative features. Choe et al. (Radiology 2019) studied 104 patients with pulmonary nodules or masses scanned on one Siemens scanner and reconstructed with B30f (soft) and B50f (sharp) kernels. Many radiomic features were not reproducible across kernels. A residual-learning CNN that converted images between kernels without sinogram data raised the concordance correlation coefficient to 0.84, with 57.4% of 702 features becoming reproducible. For nodule AI, kernel mismatch between training and deployment can change false-positive rates (sharp-kernel noise resembles small nodules), segmentation boundaries, and volume measurements, and therefore Lung-RADS category assignment near size thresholds. In iTRIALSPACE, kernel should be a separate protocol parameter. Physically grounded emulation re-filters projections (FBP with different filters) or uses validated kernel-conversion networks. Simple Gaussian blur or sharpening only approximates the change in the modulation transfer function and does not reproduce realistic noise texture.

title: CT Image Quality Metrics: NPS, MTF/TTF and Detectability (AAPM TG-233)
source: Samei et al., Med Phys 46(11):e735-e756, 2019 (AAPM TG-233)
content: Objective CT image quality is described by noise, resolution and task-based detectability. AAPM Task Group 233 ('Performance evaluation of computed tomography systems', Samei et al., Medical Physics 2019) updated CT testing for modern systems with iterative reconstruction and automatic exposure control. Noise magnitude is the standard deviation of HU in a uniform region. Noise texture is described by the noise power spectrum (NPS), the distribution of noise variance over spatial frequency, computed from the Fourier transform of mean-subtracted noise ROIs. Two images with equal standard deviation can look very different if their NPS peak frequencies differ, for example smooth vs sharp kernels, or the 'blotchy' texture of strong iterative reconstruction. Spatial resolution is described by the modulation transfer function (MTF), often summarized by the frequency at 50% or 10% MTF. Because iterative and AI reconstructions are non-linear, TG-233 emphasizes the task transfer function (TTF), measured from contrast inserts under realistic noise and contrast conditions. Task-based performance combines TTF, NPS and a task function (lesion size and contrast) into a detectability index d', for example with a non-prewhitening matched-filter observer, optionally with an eye filter. TG-233 also covers noise non-uniformity, AEC behavior and phantom recommendations. Duke's imQuest software implements TTF, NPS and d' measurement. For iTRIALSPACE, NPS and TTF are the right quantitative checks that a synthetic 'scanner profile' (vendor, kernel, dose) is realistic. Matching only mean HU and noise standard deviation is not enough. The detectability index also gives a physics-based expectation of how lesion detectability should change with size, contrast and dose.

title: Low-Dose CT: Noise, Dose Metrics and Simulation
source: NLST (NEJM 2011); McCollough et al., Med Phys 2017 (LDCT Grand Challenge); AAPM Low Dose CT Grand Challenge
content: Low-dose CT (LDCT) is the modality of lung cancer screening, validated by the NLST, where it reduced lung cancer mortality by 20% compared with chest radiography. Lung nodule detection tolerates much lower dose than soft-tissue tasks, because air-tissue contrast is high, but image noise rises as dose falls. In quantum-limited conditions, noise standard deviation scales approximately with 1/sqrt(dose): quartering the dose roughly doubles the noise standard deviation, all else equal. Dose is reported as CTDIvol (mGy) and dose-length product (DLP, mGy*cm). Tube current (mA), exposure time, tube potential (kVp), pitch and patient size all affect delivered dose and resulting noise, and automatic exposure control modulates tube current along and around the patient. Iterative and deep-learning reconstructions are used to recover image quality at low dose but change noise texture (NPS), which can affect AI models trained on FBP images.
