Realistic reduced-dose simulation is ideally done in the projection domain: add Poisson (and electronic) noise to raw data at the reduced photon fluence, then reconstruct. The 2016 NIH-AAPM-Mayo Clinic Low Dose CT Grand Challenge provided routine-dose and simulated quarter-dose data from 30 abdominal patients (10 training, 20 test) for evaluating low-dose reconstruction and denoising on liver lesion detection, and Mayo later released a broader low-dose image and projection dataset (Moen et al., Med Phys 2021). For iTRIALSPACE, 'dose level' is a core protocol axis. Even if an MVP uses image-domain noise injection, it should state that this is an approximation and ideally match the target NPS shape and noise standard deviation.

title: FDA Medical Device Development Tools (MDDT) Program
source: US FDA, Medical Device Development Tools (MDDT)
content: The FDA's Medical Device Development Tools (MDDT) program is a voluntary pathway for CDRH to qualify tools that sponsors can use in developing and evaluating medical devices. Once a tool is qualified for a specific context of use, CDRH reviewers should accept it for that context without re-justifying its validity in each submission, which reduces burden and speeds up evaluation. MDDT categories are: clinical outcome assessments (for example patient-reported outcome instruments), biomarker tests, non-clinical assessment models (NAMs: test methods that measure or predict device function or in vivo performance, including computational models, animal models and phantoms), and an 'Other' category for tools such as databases that do not fit elsewhere. Qualification depends on the context of use, a precise statement of what the tool measures or predicts and how it is used in device evaluation, supported by evidence of its validity and credibility. FDA publishes a list of qualified MDDTs with a Summary of Evidence and Basis of Qualification for each. Qualified tools span cardiovascular, neurology, ophthalmology, imaging and cross-cutting areas. An early computational example was the IMAnalytics/MRIxViP tool from ZMT/IT'IS for MR safety of implants. Relevance to iTRIALSPACE: a virtual imaging trial platform intended for regulatory use would most naturally pursue qualification as a non-clinical assessment model with a narrowly defined context of use (for example 'estimating size-dependent sensitivity of lung nodule detection software on chest CT across specified protocols'). Credibility evidence would follow the FDA computational modeling credibility framework. No generative-AI-based imaging trial tool has been verified here as MDDT-qualified.

title: FDA Guidance: Credibility of Computational Modeling and Simulation (2023)
source: US FDA final guidance, November 2023; ASME V&V 40-2018
content: In November 2023 FDA issued final guidance, 'Assessing the Credibility of Computational Modeling and Simulation in Medical Device Submissions' (draft December 2021; docket FDA-2021-D-0980). It gives a general, risk-informed framework for demonstrating that computational modeling and simulation (CM&S) evidence is credible enough to support regulatory decisions in PMA, HDE, IDE, 510(k) and De Novo submissions. It builds on concepts from the FDA-recognized consensus standard ASME V&V 40-2018 (verification and validation for computational models of medical devices). Unlike V&V 40, which assumes traditional validation experiments, it accepts other categories of credibility evidence, such as code and calculation verification, comparison with bench data, in vivo or clinical data, population-level validation, and model calibration evidence. Core concepts: define the question of interest and the context of use (COU); assess model risk from model influence (how much the decision relies on the model) and decision consequence (harm if the model is wrong); set credibility goals proportional to that risk; gather evidence; and judge adequacy. Scope is limited: the guidance applies to physics-based, mechanistic (first-principles) models and explicitly does not apply to standalone machine-learning or AI models. Implication for iTRIALSPACE: physics-based parts (CT simulation, noise or dose models, reconstruction) fit this framework directly. A generative-AI synthesis component is outside its formal scope, but the same logic (COU, model risk, validation against real data, uncertainty quantification) is the defensible way to argue credibility. Combined with the TG387 requirements of credibility, reproducibility and accessibility, it gives a good structure for a validation plan.

title: FDA AI/ML SaMD Action Plan (2021) and PCCP Guidance (2024)
source: US FDA AI/ML-Based SaMD Action Plan, January 2021; FDA final PCCP guidance, December 2024
content: In January 2021 FDA published the 'Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) Action Plan', responding to feedback on its April 2019 discussion paper on a regulatory framework for modifications to AI/ML-based SaMD. The plan listed five actions. (1) Develop the tailored regulatory framework, including draft guidance on predetermined change control plans (PCCPs). (2) Encourage harmonized Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP). (3) Support a patient-centered approach including transparency to users. (4) Support regulatory science on methods to evaluate and improve machine learning algorithms, including identifying and eliminating bias and assessing robustness. (5) Advance real-world performance monitoring pilots. Follow-on outputs included the GMLP guiding principles (October 2021), PCCP guiding principles (October 2023), transparency principles for ML-enabled devices, and the final guidance on PCCPs for AI-enabled device software functions, issued in early December 2024. A PCCP lets a manufacturer describe planned modifications (for example retraining on new data), the methodology to develop and validate them, and an impact assessment, so that changes within the plan can be implemented without a new marketing submission for each. The final guidance broadened the April 2023 draft's scope from ML-enabled to all AI-enabled devices. Relevance to iTRIALSPACE: action item 4 (robustness and bias evaluation methods) is the regulatory-science need that virtual imaging trials address. A reusable synthetic stress-test suite could also act as a fixed regression test in a PCCP's validation protocol, re-run after each model update to show performance has not degraded in any pre-specified subgroup.

title: Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP): 10 Guiding Principles
source: FDA, Health Canada, MHRA, October 2021; IMDRF N88, January 2025
content: In October 2021 the US FDA, Health Canada and the UK MHRA jointly published 10 guiding principles for Good Machine Learning Practice (GMLP) in medical device development. They are non-binding but intended to guide developers and to shape future standards. The International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) published a final document building on them in January 2025 (IMDRF AIML WG N88). The principles are: (1) multi-disciplinary expertise is leveraged throughout the total product life cycle; (2) good software engineering and security practices are implemented; (3) clinical study participants and data sets are representative of the intended patient population; (4) training data sets are independent of test sets; (5) selected reference datasets are based upon best available methods; (6) model design is tailored to the available data and reflects the intended use of the device; (7) focus is placed on the performance of the human-AI team; (8) testing demonstrates device performance during clinically relevant conditions; (9) users are provided clear, essential information; (10) deployed models are monitored for performance and re-training risks are managed. Mapping to iTRIALSPACE: principle 8 (performance under clinically relevant conditions) and principle 3 (representativeness) are what controlled synthetic cohorts test, for example sweeping vendors, kernels, doses, nodule sizes and types. Principle 4 implies synthetic test cases must not be generated from the same patients used to train the AI under test, and generative models should be checked for memorization of training scans. Principle 5 supports using precise synthetic ground truth while acknowledging its realism limits.

title: Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) Blueprint for Trustworthy AI
source: CHAI, Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation Guidance and Assurance for Healthcare, v1.0, April 2023
content: The Coalition for Health AI (CHAI) is a coalition of health systems, academic institutions, technology companies and other stakeholders, with federal agencies participating as observers. On April 4, 2023 it released the 'Blueprint for Trustworthy AI Implementation Guidance and Assurance for Healthcare' (version 1.0), a guide of about 24 pages developed with coordination involving the National Academy of Medicine. The blueprint builds on the White House OSTP 'Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights' and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0). It describes trustworthy health AI in terms of attributes including being useful, safe, accountable and transparent, explainable and interpretable, fair with harmful bias managed, secure and resilient, and privacy-enhanced. It proposed independent assurance labs where health systems and developers could submit AI tools for evaluation, and it presented itself as a step toward future assurance standards rather than a finished standard. It is not a regulation. For iTRIALSPACE, the CHAI framing supports positioning virtual imaging trials as an assurance tool. Subgroup and robustness reports (performance by lesion size, location, nodule type and acquisition protocol) provide the evidence on safety, fairness (managing harmful bias across populations and sites) and transparency that assurance processes look for. An assurance-oriented report should state the intended use of the AI under test, the synthetic cohort's design and known realism limits, the metrics with confidence intervals, and where performance falls below pre-specified thresholds.

title: iTRIALSPACE: Programmable Virtual Lesion Trials for Controlled Evaluation of Lung CT Models
source: Tushar, Momy, Lo, Rubin. arXiv:2605.05761, May 2026
content: iTRIALSPACE (Fakrul Islam Tushar, Umme Hafsa Momy, Joseph Y. Lo, Geoffrey D. Rubin; arXiv May 2026) is a programmable evaluation framework for controlled assessment of lung CT models. Its motivation: standard benchmarks are static retrospective collections that entangle lesion size, lobe prevalence, anatomy and acquisition context, making it difficult to determine what structurally drives model accuracy. iTRIALSPACE composes real clinical CTs and lesion profiles into controlled virtual lesion trials through a four-stage pipeline: (1) multidataset nodule profiling, (2) explicit trial specification, (3) anatomy-aware mask insertion, and (4) ControlNet-conditioned CT synthesis. The framework is built on a unified 54-attribute nodule-profile dataset spanning 13,140 annotated nodules from seven public CT sources and is instantiated as 13 trial modes. It was evaluated in a 55,469-sample Virtual Lesion Study spanning three medical vision-language models (VLMs), four spatial-guidance conditions and three clinical tasks. Across all 13 modes the synthetic substrate remained within the real-to-real FID baseline, and synthetic performance rankings transferred strongly to real clinical data (Spearman rho = 0.93, p < 1e-15). Controlled trial modes exposed findings unavailable to fixed-distribution benchmarks, including shortcut-driven size-prediction collapse under lobe-equalized sampling, and host-to-donor variance ratios of 8.9x and 3.3x in twin-cross analysis. The authors position iTRIALSPACE as auditable evaluation infrastructure for controlled, falsifiable testing beyond static retrospective benchmarks.

title: NodMAISI: Nodule-Oriented Medical AI for Synthetic Imaging
source: Tushar, Samei, Rudin, Lo. arXiv:2512.18038, Dec 2025
content: NodMAISI (Fakrul Islam Tushar, Ehsan Samei, Cynthia Rudin, Joseph Y. Lo; arXiv December 2025) is an anatomically constrained, nodule-oriented CT synthesis and augmentation framework. Motivation: small pulmonary nodules, critical to lung cancer screening, remain underrepresented and inconsistently curated in public datasets. It is trained on a unified multi-source cohort of 7,042 patients, 8,841 CTs and 14,444 nodules, and integrates (i) a standardized curation and annotation pipeline linking each CT with organ masks and nodule-level annotations, (ii) a ControlNet-conditioned rectified-flow generator built on MAISI-v2's foundational blocks to enforce anatomy- and lesion-consistent synthesis, and (iii) lesion-aware augmentation that perturbs nodule masks (controlled shrinkage) while preserving surrounding anatomy to generate paired CT variants. Across six public test datasets NodMAISI improved distributional fidelity relative to MAISI-v2 (real-to-synthetic FID 1.18-2.99 vs 1.69-5.21). In lesion detectability analysis with a MONAI nodule detector, it substantially increased average sensitivity and more closely matched clinical scans (IMD-CT 0.69 vs 0.39; DLCS24 0.63 vs 0.20), with the largest gains for sub-centimeter nodules, where MAISI-v2 frequently failed to reproduce the conditioned lesion. For nodule malignancy classification trained on LUNA25 and externally evaluated on LUNA16, LNDbv4 and DLCS24, NodMAISI augmentation improved AUC by 0.07-0.11 with 20% or less clinical data and by 0.12-0.21 at 10%, narrowing the performance gap under data scarcity.

title: Tri-Reader: Open-Access Multi-Stage AI Pipeline for First-Pass Lung Nodule Annotation
source: Tushar, Lo. arXiv:2601.19380, Jan 2026
content: Tri-Reader (Fakrul Islam Tushar, Joseph Y. Lo; arXiv January 2026) is a comprehensive, freely available pipeline built from multiple open-access models trained on public datasets. It integrates lung segmentation, nodule detection and malignancy classification into a unified tri-stage workflow for first-pass lung nodule annotation in screening CT. The pipeline is designed to prioritize sensitivity while reducing the candidate burden for human annotators. To assess accuracy and generalizability across diverse practices, Tri-Reader was evaluated on multiple internal and external datasets against expert annotations and dataset-provided reference standards. It illustrates a data-centric approach: using open models to accelerate curation of the nodule annotations that downstream synthesis and evaluation frameworks depend on.
